farraa:1-1.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَٱللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ إِنَّ ٱلْمُنَافِقِينَ لَكَاذِبُونَ﴾.
Someone may say: They bore witness for the Prophet ﷺ, saying: ﴿وَٱللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ إِنَّكَ لَرَسُولُهُ﴾, so how did Allah call them liars?
It is said: He only gave the lie to what they concealed in themselves, because they concealed hypocrisy. Just as He did not accept their faith although they displayed it, so He made them liars, because they concealed something other than what they displayed.

farraa:10-10.t:
His saying: ﴿فَأَصَّدَّقَ وَأَكُن مِّنَ ٱلصَّالِحِينَ﴾.
It is asked: How is (وأكن) jussive when it is joined back to an accusative verb? The answer to that is that if the فاء had not been on أصدق, it would have been jussive; so when you joined (وأكنْ) back, it was joined to the underlying sense of the verb as it would be without the فاء. Whoever keeps the واو joins it back to the overt verb and so makes it accusative; and that is in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "وأكونَ من الصالحين".
Its accusative is also permissible in our reading even though the واو is not in it [in the script], because the Arabs sometimes drop the واو in some spellings, just as they dropped the ألف from سليمن and the like. I have seen in some of the codices of ʿAbd Allāh: فقولا written فقلا, without واو.

farraa:4-4.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِذَا رَأَيْتَهُمْ تُعْجِبُكَ أَجْسَامُهُمْ﴾.
Some of the Arabs put the verb in the jussive after إذا, saying: إذا تقم أقمْ (when you stand, I stand). One of them recited to me:
وإذا نطاوِعْ أمرَ سادتِنا * لا يَثْنِنا جُبن ولا بُخْلُ
(When we obey the command of our lords, neither cowardice nor miserliness turns us back.)
Another said:
واستغْنِ ما أغناك ربُّك بالغِنى * وإذا تُصبْك خصاصةٌ فتجمَّل
(Be content with wealth as long as your Lord makes you rich; and when poverty strikes you, bear it with dignity.)
But most usage with it is the nominative [indicative], because it is in the manner of an adverbial (ṣifa, i.e. ẓarf), do you not see that you say: الرُّطب إذا اشتد الحر (fresh dates are when the heat grows intense), meaning at that time. Since it is in the position of an adverbial, it is a complement (ṣila) of the verb that comes before it, or of what comes after the verb that follows it. So the poet said:
وإذا تكون شديدةٌ أُدْعَى لها * وإذا يحاسُ الحَيْسُ يُدْعَى جُندُبُ
(When there is a hardship, I am called for it; and when the ḥays [a date-and-butter dish] is mixed, Jundub is called.)
His saying: ﴿كَأَنَّهُمْ خُشُبٌ مُّسَنَّدَةٌ﴾.
Al-Aʿmash read it light [خُشْب], and Ismāʿīl ibn Jaʿfar al-Madanī, from his companions, and ʿĀṣim read it heavy [خُشُب]. Whoever reads it heavy, it is as if he pluralised خشبة as خِشاب and then pluralised that again [199/b] and so made it heavy, just as they said: ثمار and ثُمُر. And if you wish, you may pluralise it — it being خشبة — as خُشُب, and make it light or heavy, just as they said: البدَنة, البُدُن and البُدْن, and الأَكَم and الأُكُم.
The Arabs pluralise some words having the form of خشبة, I think, on the pattern fuʿl; among them: أجمة and أُجْم, بَدَنة and بُدْن, أكَمة and أُكْم.
And of this kind among the weak (muʿtall) words: ساحة and سُوح, ساق and سُوق, عانة and عُون, لابة and لُوب, قارة and قور, and حياة and حِيّ. Al-ʿAjjāj said:
* ولو ترى إذ الحياة حِىّ *
(If only you had seen when life was [full of] living things.)
It should have been حُوِيّ, but its first letter was given kasra so that the ياء would not change into a واو, just as they said: بِيض and عِين.
His saying: ﴿يَحْسَبُونَ كُلَّ صَيْحَةٍ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾.
Out of cowardice and fear. Then He said: "هم العدو" and did not say: هم الأعداء; and all of that is correct.

farraa:5-5.t:
His saying: ﴿لَوَّوْاْ رُءُوسَهُمْ﴾.
They moved them in mockery of the Prophet ﷺ and his call. Some of the people of Medina read: "لَوَوْا رءوسهم" without doubling.

farraa:7-8.t:
His saying: ﴿هُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ لاَ تُنفِقُواْ عَلَىٰ مَنْ عِندَ رَسُولِ ٱللَّهِ﴾.
The Prophet ﷺ was on one of his campaigns, and a man of the Muslims called Jiʿāl and another of the hypocrites met at a watering place and jostled each other over it; Jiʿāl struck him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy saw it and became angry, and said: We only brought these people into our home to be struck — what is the matter with them? May Allah leave them to Jiʿāl and Jiʿāl's kind! Then he said: You — if only you had withheld food from the companions of this man, they would have dispersed from him and broken away. That is His saying: ﴿هُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ لاَ تُنفِقُواْ عَلَىٰ مَنْ عِندَ رَسُولِ ٱللَّهِ حَتَّىٰ يَنفَضُّواْ﴾. Then ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy said: ﴿لَئِن رَّجَعْنَآ إِلَى ٱلْمَدِينَةِ لَيُخْرِجَنَّ ٱلأَعَزُّ مِنْهَا ٱلأَذَلَّ﴾. Zayd ibn Arqam heard it and told the Prophet ﷺ, and the Qurʾān came down: ﴿وَلِلَّهِ ٱلْعِزَّةُ وَلِرَسُولِهِ وَلِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾.
It is permissible in reading: "لَيُخْرَجَنَّ الأعزُّ منها الأذلَّ", as if you said: the mighty one will surely be driven out of it humiliated [i.e. الأذلّ as ḥāl (circumstantial)]. Some read: لنُخْرِجَن الأعزَّ منها الأذل, i.e.: we will surely drive out the one who is mighty in his own estimation, humiliated.
[Translator's note: «إنكم لم منعتم» is as printed; it is understood as «إنكم لو منعتم» ("if only you had withheld").]
